flashcard_questions.q: Which euphemism do the pigs use for cutting the animals' rations?
Which term means presenting something as less significant than it really is?
What is Animal Farm proclaimed to be in Chapter Nine?
flashcard_questions.a: A Republic, with Napoleon as the only candidate for President.

flashcard_questions.q: Which injury does Boxer never fully recover from?
flashcard_questions.a: A split hoof, sustained at the Battle of the Windmill.

flashcard_questions.q: What retirement age had Boxer been promised?
Which word means sadness and compassion at another's suffering?
Which lettering does Benjamin read on the side of the van?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler, Willingdon.’

flashcard_questions.q: Which words does Benjamin shout when he reads the van's lettering?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘Fools! Fools! Do you not see what is written on the side of that van?’

flashcard_questions.q: Which quotation shows Boxer too weak to kick his way out of the van?
What explanation does Squealer give for the knacker's name on the van?
flashcard_questions.a: The vet had bought it and not yet painted over the old lettering.

flashcard_questions.q: What do the pigs buy with the money from Boxer's sale?
Which social class does Boxer represent in the allegory?
flashcard_questions.a: The proletariat, the loyal hardworking masses.

flashcard_questions.q: Which motto shows Boxer's blind faith in the leadership?
Which cynical motto shows Benjamin always expected the revolution to fail?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘Donkeys live a long time. None of you has ever seen a dead donkey’.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Orwell warn through Benjamin's political apathy?
flashcard_questions.a: That silence from those who see through the lies enables tyranny.

notes: 15 cards: 7 character or theme to quotation, 3 term-to-definition phrased 'Which term/word means…' (understatement, pathos) plus the euphemism example, 3 plot-detail cards (retirement age, split hoof, whisky), 2 significance cards (Boxer as proletariat, Benjamin's apathy). Split Boxer's two mottos into one card each direction would have duplicated, so only 'Napoleon is always right' is kept as the blind-faith card. Dropped privileges, knacker and betrayal as glossary cards — all three are carried by the van and whisky cards.
